Role Summary
About the role
The British Museum is seeking a Project Curator to join the department of Africa, Oceania and the Americas.  Working on the
African Histories and Heritage Programme
, you will play a leading role in the delivery of the project: ‘Reconnecting Eastern African Collections and Histories’ (REACH).
REACH is a new 4-year research and education project aiming to significantly expand knowledge of the British Museum’s Eastern Africa collection and increase its impact. This project will produce an object-based history of the ivory caravan trade and imposition of colonial rule (c1800-1914) in Eastern Africa. Working in collaboration with an international network of partner museums and community stakeholders in Tanzania, Kenya and Uganda, the team will generate new knowledge about museum collections, build strong relationships between partners and share knowledge in East Africa through bespoke schools’ programmes and other activities.
You will play a vital role in connecting people with the collection, expanding curatorial practice and advancing interpretations of African histories and heritage at the British Museum.
About you
You are an experienced curator or researcher with a commitment to ethical, collaborative and community-centred approaches to museum collections. Working closely with the Project Lead, you will bring strong research expertise, cultural awareness and the ability to build meaningful partnerships across the British Museum and with colleagues and communities in East Africa.

Job Introduction
Creativity, innovation and forward thinking infuses every aspect of Tate and we approach corporate fundraising in the same way! As a result, Tate has a long history of generating ground-breaking partnerships and delivering significant return on investment for its Corporate Partners.

You will oversee the internal and external project management of each partnership. Through liaising regularly with relevant Tate departments, as well as working with and motivating the Corporate Partnerships Officers, you’ll help ensure we create and deliver interesting, cutting edge and competitive opportunities for our corporate partners. You will be responsible for cultivating new prospects and identifying partners with the capacity to be repeat funders. You’ll also work to devise and implement a strategic and innovative approach to securing future business.
As well as experience managing b2b relationships you should have an innate ability to build an inclusive, respectful and collaborative culture within a team. You should also have excellent organisational and project management skills as well as a flair for juggling a busy workload to meet deadlines. About us
The Department of Medical and Molecular Genetics at King’s College London is at the forefront of human genetics research. We are part of the School of Basic and Medical Biosciences within the Faculty of Life Sciences and Medicine at King’s College London. This post is based in the Department of Medical and Molecular Genetics and supervised by Professor Matthew Brown, working in close collaboration with Professor Emma Duncan of the Department of Twin Research & Genetic Epidemiology. Their collaborative research group focuses on unlocking the genetic basis of common and rare bone and joint diseases, including ankylosing spondylitis and related conditions. We have access to state-of-the-art facilities and are embedded within a global network of collaborators.

Supervised by Professor Matthew Brown (Medical and Molecular Genetics) and working closely with Professor Emma Duncan (Twin Research & Genetic Epidemiology), you will harness advanced bioinformatics approaches to decode the genetic underpinnings of these conditions. title: Research Assistant/associate in development of 4D image processing methods (Fixed Term)
description:
The post holder will be located in Central Cambridge, UK.
Computed tomography (CT) has transformed fields by enabling non-destructive three-dimensional (3D) imaging. However, conventional CT is fundamentally limited by acquisition speed: high-quality 3D reconstruction typically requires thousands of X-ray radiographs acquired over a full specimen rotation, taking minutes to hours. This makes CT unsuitable for fast, transient phenomena such as additive manufacturing, impact, fracture and high-rate deformation.
We are launching an ambitious research programme to overcome this limitation and establish new approaches for X-ray tomography of rapidly evolving processes. Combining advances in X-ray hardware, computational imaging, machine learning and mechanics, the project aims to reconstruct the three-dimensional evolution of materials during dynamic deformation, moving beyond static CT towards true four-dimensional imaging in space and time.
We seek an outstanding Research Associate/Research Assistant to play a leading role in developing the computational foundations of this programme. The successful candidate will develop reconstruction and image-processing methods for highly under sampled, dynamically evolving X-ray datasets, including approaches based on neural radiance fields (NeRFs), neural representations and related state-of-the-art computational imaging techniques.
A central challenge will be to combine X-ray measurements with physical knowledge of deformation processes. The project therefore offers significant scope to develop new physics-informed and data-driven approaches coupling computational imaging with models of material deformation, with considerable freedom to shape the computational research programme.
The computational work will be closely integrated with new laboratory X-ray hardware and high-rate mechanical experiments. Experience or interest in continuum mechanics and computational solid mechanics would therefore be advantageous. Familiarity with

title: Research Associate (Blouet and Káradóttir Labs)
description:
Oligodendrocyte progenitor cells are now recognised as stem cells of the adult brain, recruited for learning and repair throughout life. This project aims at testing innovative ways of recruiting oligodendrocyte lineage cells in neurodegenerative disease by targeting metabolic pathways.
This post is part of a new collaborative research programme at the University of Cambridge based across the laboratories of Professor Clémence Blouet (Institute of Metabolic Science) and Professor Ragnhildur Thóra Káradóttir (Cambridge Stem Cell Institute; Director of the MS Society Cambridge Centre for Myelin Repair). The project is funded by Eli Lilly and will test the idea that targeting incretin receptor agonists can promote remyelination and support brain repair in progressive multiple sclerosis.
The successful candidate will work across both laboratories. The project will involve focal demyelinating lesion models, stereotaxic surgery and pharmacological interventions, in vivo recordings of neuronal activity, histology and imaging, and single-nucleus transcriptomics.
This is a unique opportunity to work at the interface of metabolic science and neuroscience in a collaborative translational environment, with access to state-of-the-art facilities across the Cambridge Stem Cell Institute, the Institute of Metabolic Science, and the wider Cambridge Biomedical Campus.
Requirements:
Applicants should hold a PhD in neuroscience or a related discipline. A strong background in in vivo rodent work is essential. Experience with several of the required techniques is important, including stereotaxic surgery, histology, imaging, or electrophysiological techniques, particularly in vivo. We will provide training where needed . The successful candidate must be highly organised, able to work both independently and collaboratively, and have strong analytical and communication skills.

User Researcher
We care for millions of public records spanning government, courts and parliament. Our oldest records are from over a thousand years ago. We are committed to making these collections accessible through high-quality digital services for future generations.
As a User Researcher, you will help teams understand user needs and behaviours through evidence-based research. Using a range of qualitative and quantitative research methods, you will generate insights that inform service design, support decision-making and ensure our products and services meet the needs of diverse users. You will work closely with multidisciplinary teams to identify opportunities, shape solutions and advocate for users throughout the product lifecycle.
This is a unique opportunity to undertake user research in an environment focused on complex information services rather than purely transactional services. You will work alongside experts from across our collections and research communities while contributing to the future access of public records through our digital services.
This role would suit someone who is curious, analytical and motivated by solving complex problems through research and evidence.

Royal Museums Greenwich is a collection of diverse historical sites. The sites are the National Maritime Museum, Cutty Sark, the Royal Observatory, and the Queen’s House. Each of these sites has a unique identity and a common purpose to serve our communities, through sharing our collections and expertise. We are a place to explore the sea, space, art and history, and our strategy ‘Charting Our Course’ puts people at the core of its success.
The Role
If you are passionate about the role Museums play in the learning journeys of children and young people, then this is the role for you. We are looking for a dynamic individual to work with schools and teachers to support and inspire collections-based learning at the National Maritime Museum and the Queen’s House. You will lead on the development, delivery and resourcing of historical enquiry programmes from early years to post 16, giving all school learners a high-quality experience that is unique to our sites. You will also nurture relationships with key internal and external stakeholders, ensuring that audience voice is embedded into everything we do.
The successful candidate will have a proven track record of engaging children and young people using museum collections and a great understanding of the needs of school learners and teachers. Effective time management and written and verbal presentation skills are also required. This role involves working with histories relating to empire and the transatlantic trade of enslaved people so experience of culturally sensitive approaches to exploring these topics is essential. It’s a fast-paced and rewarding role that puts learning at the centre of the Museum.
